items.title: Syllogism — Venn method, either-or & possibility
items.body:
## Method

Assume all statements are 100% true and draw the **least possible** Venn diagram. A definite conclusion must hold in *every* possible diagram; a **possibility** conclusion holds if it is true in *any one* diagram.

## Quantifier → diagram

| Statement | Meaning |
|---|---|
| All A are B | A wholly inside B (definite converse: Some B are A) |
| Some A are B | A and B overlap |
| Some A are not B | part of A lies outside B |
| No A is B | A and B disjoint (No B is A too) |

## Either-Or (complementary pairs)

When two conclusions have the **same subject & predicate**, are **individually false**, and form the pair **Some + No** or **All + Some-not**, the answer is *Either I or II follows*.

## Worked example

Statements: All bottles are black; Some black are white. Conclusions: I. All blacks are bottles; II. Some blacks are not bottles. Both are only *possible* (individually false) and form the All + Some-not pair → **Either I or II follows**.

## Common traps

- Treating a possible conclusion as definite.
- Reading 'Some + Some-not' or 'All + No' as an either-or pair (they are NOT).
- Forgetting 'Only a few A are B' = Some are + Some are not (both definite).
keyPoints: Always draw the least possible Venn diagram; a definite conclusion must hold in every diagram.
'All A are B' gives the definite converse 'Some B are A'.
Either-Or pairs are only Some+No and All+Some-not, with same subject/predicate and both individually false.
A possibility conclusion is true if it holds in any one valid diagram.
'Only a few A are B' means Some A are B AND Some A are not B (both definitely true).
If all statements are positive, all negative definite conclusions are false, and vice versa.

items.title: Coded inequalities — decoding & either-or
items.body:
## Method

First **decode** any symbols into <, >, ≤, ≥, =, then combine only when every link points the **same direction**. A relation is definite only if the chain is unbroken and one-directional.

## Direction rules

| Chain | Definite conclusion |
|---|---|
| P > Q > R / P > Q ≥ R / P = Q > R | P > R |
| P < Q < R / P < Q ≤ R / P = Q < R | P < R |
| P ≥ Q ≥ R / P = Q ≥ R | P ≥ R (P > R or P = R) |
| P ≤ Q ≤ R | P ≤ R |
| P < Q > R (opposite arrows meet) | No conclusion |

A single strict '>' in an otherwise '≥/=' chain makes the end relation strict '>'.

## Either-Or

When two elements can't be fixed and the two conclusions form **≤ + >** (or **> + ≤**) on the same pair, both are individually false but together exhaust all cases → *Either/Or*.

## Worked example

H = T > U ≤ I: the '>' and '≤' meet at U, so H vs I is undetermined. 'H > I' and 'H ≤ I' → **Either I or II follows**.

## Common traps

- Concluding a strict '>' from a '≥' link (equality is allowed).
- Combining across opposite-facing arrows (P < Q > R gives nothing).
keyPoints: Decode symbols to <,>,≤,≥,= before combining any relations.
Combine only same-direction links; opposite arrows meeting at an element break the relation.
A '≥' link can never yield a strict '>' conclusion by itself.
One strict '>' in a ≥/= chain forces the overall relation to be '>'.
Inequality either-or pairs are ≤+> and >+≤ on the same two elements, both individually false.

items.title: Logical Venn — representation & region counts
items.body:
## Representation

Choose the diagram from the class relationship: a strict 'is-a' chain (Pigeon ⊂ Bird ⊂ Living thing) = **nested/concentric** circles; two co-ordinate subclasses of one class (Gold, Silver ⊂ Metal) = **separate** circles inside it; classes that only sometimes coincide (Doctors, Females) = **overlapping** circles.

## Numerical formula

Two sets: **n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)**; *neither* = Total − n(A ∪ B).

Three sets: **n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A)+n(B)+n(C) − n(A∩B) − n(B∩C) − n(A∩C) + n(A∩B∩C)**.

## Worked example

100 students, 60 tea, 50 coffee, 30 both. At least one = 60 + 50 − 30 = 80; **neither = 100 − 80 = 20**.

## Common traps

- Forgetting to subtract the overlap (double-counting 'both').
- Confusing 'only A' (n(A) − n(A∩B)) with n(A).
keyPoints: Nested circles = strict subset chain; separate circles = disjoint co-ordinate classes; overlap = partial coincidence.
Two-set union: n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B).
Neither = Total − n(A∪B).
Only-A region = n(A) − n(A∩B); subtract overlaps to avoid double counting.
Three-set count adds back the triple overlap n(A∩B∩C).
items.source: APPSC GK — Logical Reasoning: Logical Venn & Venn Diagram Problems

items.title: Seating, floor & grouping puzzles — approach
items.body:
## General approach

Place **definite clues first** (ends, fixed floors, 'directly opposite'), then fit relative clues ('immediately right/below', 'between'). Keep a slot grid and eliminate.

## Linear rows

Facing **north**: person's left = your left. Facing **south**: left/right flip. 'Between X and Y' fixes order once one end is known.

## Circular tables

Facing the **centre**: a person's left is clockwise-neighbour's side; facing **outward** it reverses. In an n-seat circle the person opposite seat i sits at seat **i + n/2**.

## Floor puzzles

Number floors bottom = 1 to top = n; 'immediately above/below' = adjacent floors; 'topmost/ground' are hard anchors.

## Grouping & selection

Count with combinations C(n,r); apply constraints by **subtracting** invalid groups (e.g. 'A and B never together', 'at least one woman').

## Common traps

- Mixing up left/right for south-facing or outward-facing people.
- Assuming adjacency when only 'near' (not 'immediately next') is stated.
keyPoints: Anchor definite clues (ends, fixed floors, opposite) before relative clues.
North-facing: person's left = your left; south-facing reverses.
In an n-seat circle, seat opposite i is seat i + n/2.
Floor 'immediately above/below' means adjacent floors; top/ground are hard anchors.
Grouping: use C(n,r) and subtract groups that break constraints.
'Near' is not the same as 'immediately next to' — do not assume adjacency.
items.source: APPSC GK — Logical Reasoning: Seating, Floor & Grouping puzzles

items.title: Statement-based verbal reasoning — arguments, assumptions, conclusions, inferences
items.body:
## Statement & Arguments

**Strong** = relevant + directly related to the issue + real practical import. **Weak** = trivial, ambiguous, superficial, or merely restating the question.

## Statement & Assumptions

An assumption is something **taken for granted** for the statement to hold. Test by **negation**: if denying it collapses the statement, it is implicit. Reject assumptions that are extreme, comparative-opinion, or bring in outside facts.

## Statement & Conclusions

Accept **moderate, hedged** conclusions ('may', 'likely') that follow reasonably; reject **absolute** claims ('always', 'completely', 'never') and anything needing facts beyond the statement.

## Statement & Inferences

An inference must be a **logically certain** deduction from the data, adding nothing external. Distinguish **percentage points** (75 − 60 = 15) from **percent change** (15/60 = 25%).

## Common traps

- Marking an extreme conclusion/course as valid.
- Treating a debatable value-judgement as an implicit assumption.
keyPoints: Strong argument = relevant + directly related + real practical import; weak = trivial/ambiguous/restates question.
Assumption test: negate it — if the statement fails, it is implicit.
Reject extreme, comparative-opinion, or outside-fact assumptions.
Conclusions: accept hedged ('may/likely'), reject absolute ('always/never/completely').
Inference must be logically certain from the passage, adding no external data.
Percentage points (75−60=15) differ from percent increase (15/60=25%).

items.title: Assertion-Reason, Cause-Effect & Course of Action frameworks
items.body:
## Assertion & Reason (standard 4 options)

1. Both A and R true, **R correctly explains A**.
2. Both A and R true, but R is **NOT** the correct explanation.
3. A true, R false.
4. A false, R true.

Method: judge each statement's truth first, then test whether R is the *cause* of A.

## Cause & Effect

Identify which event realistically **triggers** the other and check the **time order**. Options usually include: I cause/II effect; II cause/I effect; independent causes; both effects of a common cause.

## Course of Action

A valid course of action is **feasible, proportionate, and improves** the situation. Reject actions that are extreme, escapist, or create bigger problems.

## Worked cues

- Water boils lower at altitude *because* pressure falls → A-R option 1.
- Petrol price rises → public-transport use rises → I is cause, II is effect.
- Many fail Maths → arrange remedial coaching (valid); removing Maths (invalid, extreme).
keyPoints: A-R: decide truth of A and R separately, then whether R explains A.
A-R option 1 requires R to be the actual cause of A, not just co-true.
Cause-Effect: find the realistic trigger and check chronological order.
Course of action must be feasible, proportionate and improve the situation.
Reject extreme or escapist courses of action (e.g. removing a core subject).
items.source: APPSC GK — Verbal Reasoning: Assertion-Reason, Cause & Effect, Course of Action

items.title: Truth-functional logic, cause-elimination & indeterminacy traps
items.body:
## Falsifying a disjunction or conditional (UPSC CSAT favourite)

| Claim | It is FALSE only when |
|---|---|
| 'A or B' (inclusive) | BOTH A and B are false |
| 'A and B' | at least ONE of A, B is false |
| 'If P then Q' | P is TRUE and Q is FALSE |

- An inclusive 'or' is still true when both happen; only 'neither' breaks it.
- A conditional is never falsified by a false antecedent (it is vacuously true).

## Cause-elimination / data logic

Given who consumed what and who was affected, the **cause** is the single item that is common to **every affected** case AND absent from **every unaffected** case. One healthy consumer eliminates an item.

Worked cue: sick ate {rice,curd},{rice,salad},{rice,juice}; healthy ate {curd,salad},{juice,salad}. Only *rice* is in all sick and no healthy set ⇒ rice is the cause.

## Indeterminacy ('cannot be determined')

When the data is consistent with **more than one** answer, the correct response is *nothing definite can be said*. Test-writers dress an underdetermined split (e.g. gender of a music-free subset drawn from 30 non-music men + some non-music women) as though a definite option existed.

## Common traps

- Reading inclusive 'or' as exclusive (marking 'both' as a falsifier).
- Treating a false-antecedent case as violating a conditional.
- Picking a definite-sounding option when the data underdetermines it.
keyPoints: 'A or B' is false only when both are false; 'if P then Q' is false only when P is true and Q is false.
A false antecedent leaves a conditional vacuously true — it cannot falsify the rule.
Cause = item common to every affected case and absent from every unaffected case; one healthy consumer eliminates it.
When data fits several answers, the correct choice is 'cannot be determined'.
Inclusive 'or' stays true when both parts occur — only 'neither' breaks it.
items.source: UPSC CSE (CSAT) 2016 patterns (via UPSCprep); APPSC GK — Verbal Reasoning: Logic
